notes.title: Use Optional for a meaningful, non-exceptional missing value
notes.core: Represent an ordinary possibly-absent result with a non-null Optional return when callers genuinely need to choose an absence policy; keep collections and failed operations as separate contracts.
rules: An Optional-returning function must never itself return null; use empty(), of() or ofNullable() according to the input contract.
Favor orElseGet for expensive fallback work: orElse evaluates its fallback expression even when a value exists.
Use map, flatMap, filter and stream to compose presence-aware operations without unsafe get() calls.
Prefer an empty collection/array for a successful zero-result query, not an Optional wrapping the collection as a default design.
Use OptionalInt, OptionalLong and OptionalDouble where primitive absence has useful meaning and avoid unnecessary boxed Optional<Integer>.
Treat exceptional failures and absent normal results differently, and document which cases correspond to each.
nuance: Returning Optional is a design trade-off with possible allocation and indirection costs; measure before optimizing, and never claim universal speed advantages.
An Optional is usually not a suitable key or value in a collection: it can create two meanings of absent and complicate lookups.
Optional as an object field is occasionally justified by complex domain modeling, not categorically forbidden.
Optional.orElseThrow() without a supplier is available in Java 21; this does not make get() safe on empty containers.
Optional.map converts a null mapper result to an empty Optional; flatMap expects a non-null Optional result and can reject null.
An Optional return may force clients to address absence, but Java permits intentionally ignoring it; code review still matters.
notes.misconception: An Optional wrapper automatically makes every null and missing-data scenario safe, including collections and internal fields.
notes.production_context: A fraud-scoring cache returns Optional<RiskRule> for an unknown rule ID, an empty List for a valid query with no matches, and an explicit error for a failed remote lookup.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 provides no-arg orElseThrow(), Optional.stream() and primitive optional specializations; absence semantics from the Java 9-era text still apply. Benchmark allocation claims on the current JDK.

notes.title: Publish API contracts that can survive implementation changes
notes.core: Document the observable behavior of every exported API element, including preconditions, return meaning, failure policy and concurrency assumptions; validate both generated HTML and its rendering.
rules: Give public types and methods distinct concise summary lines that describe the contract instead of internal implementation details.
Document every public method parameter, return value and relevant thrown exception, including invalid input preconditions.
Document generic type parameters and public enum constants; use package-info.java and module-info.java when appropriate.
Use {@code} for literal source snippets and {@literal} for prose containing HTML-sensitive characters, and inspect the generated HTML.
Explain thread-safety, mutability, optional absence and serialization contracts when clients need to know them.
When inheritance is deliberately supported, document extension hooks and self-use behavior separately from the client contract.
nuance: Java 21 Javadoc generates HTML5 by default; do not reproduce historic -html5 switches as mandatory current guidance.
Javadoc doclint can detect many broken links/tags but cannot prove behavioral promises are correct; compare documentation to tests.
Java 21 supports @implSpec and other inline documentation tags; check rendering with the installed tool rather than trusting old Java 9 configuration advice.
Contract descriptions need not promise internal algorithm or time complexity unless those are intentional public guarantees.
A public default constructor cannot receive its own explicit source comment; define a documented constructor if construction semantics matter.
Inherited docs can reduce repetition but should be checked against subtype-specific preconditions and behavior.
notes.misconception: A clean Javadoc build guarantees that the API behavior, errors and compatibility guarantees are documented accurately.
notes.production_context: An exported alert-pagination API documents inclusive/exclusive bounds, empty-result behavior, ownership of returned lists, exceptions and whether it is safe to call concurrently.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 Javadoc defaults to HTML5 and supports doclint and modern standard tags; the book’s Java 9-era generator switches and defaults must not be copied uncritically.

notes.title: Keep values visible only within their meaningful lifetime
notes.core: Narrow the lexical scope of temporary state by declaring it close to first use, preferring initialized locals and loop-bound variables, so a name cannot accidentally influence an unrelated operation.
rules: Initialize local variables where practical at first use instead of declaring them at method entry.
Use for-loop or enhanced-for variables local to the loop when state is not needed after iteration.
Split independent work into focused methods when unrelated locals remain visible too long.
Use a standard indexed loop only when index, replacement or synchronized traversal is truly required.
Do not cache loop bounds that can change during traversal; only hoist values proven stable.
Use try-with-resources for closable resource lifetime, while acknowledging that a surrounding catch block can require an outer result declaration.
nuance: A narrow lexical scope is not the same as object lifetime or thread safety; a captured mutable reference may still escape.
Java 21 pattern variables have flow-sensitive scopes; don’t assume they can be reused outside valid branches.
The local var keyword infers a static type and does not weaken lexical scope; clear initializer types still matter.
Early initialization can be harmful when an operation must first establish a precondition or a resource should open later.
A loop bound can be cached when stable and expensive, but never if doing so changes semantics of a mutable collection.
Separate return/error paths may naturally keep values in distinct scopes without forcing pointless extra blocks.
notes.misconception: A variable declared at the top of a method is safer because every branch can reach it.
notes.production_context: Two sequential paginated event scans must not accidentally consult the first scan’s exhausted iterator or cached limit when deciding whether a second scan has records.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 var and flow-scoped instanceof pattern variables complement the old declare-near-use rule; loop-bound scoping and definite assignment remain enforced.

notes.title: Iterate by element when index control adds no value
notes.core: Use enhanced-for over Iterable values or arrays when only elements are needed; reserve explicit iterators or indexes for mutation, coordinated iteration and positional operations.
rules: Use enhanced-for for ordinary read-only iteration over collections and arrays, especially nested independent axes.
Do not advance a nested outer iterator from an inner loop; preserve outer element for the entire inner traversal.
Prefer removeIf for predicate-based destructive filtering when the collection supports it, otherwise use Iterator.remove safely.
Use a ListIterator or index when changing positions or replacing elements; enhanced-for is not an element replacement API.
When aligning two sequences element-by-element, use explicit iterators or indexes and decide what unequal lengths mean.
Expose Iterable for domain containers that support safe traversal, even if they do not implement Collection.
nuance: Enhanced-for does not guarantee thread safety or permit arbitrary structural modification during iteration.
An Iterator.remove operation is not supported by every iterator; check the concrete collection contract.
Java 21 SequencedCollection and reversed views offer order-related conveniences but do not make two independent iterables zip automatically.
A stream does not implement Iterable; choose an adapter or a different API shape if language-level enhanced-for is required.
An indexed loop remains appropriate when indexes carry domain semantics or are needed for in-place array transformation.
Performance equivalence across all custom Iterable implementations is not guaranteed; profile particular implementations if hot.
notes.misconception: Enhanced-for always permits safe removal or replacement and can naturally zip two collections of different lengths.
notes.production_context: A payment processor combines regions with alert severities using two independent enhanced-for loops, but uses an explicit Iterator to remove expired listeners.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 preserves enhanced-for over Iterable and arrays, adds sequenced-collection APIs, and still does not make Stream directly Iterable.

notes.title: Prefer tested JDK facilities over ad-hoc utility reinvention
notes.core: Search the JDK for established solutions before writing custom utility algorithms; check contracts, security requirements and current JDK capabilities rather than carrying over outdated library recommendations.
rules: Prefer a standard bounded random-number API over modulo/Math.abs approximations that can overflow or bias results.
Use SecureRandom for security-sensitive tokens and salts; convenience pseudo-random generators are not cryptographic.
Use established collection, I/O, time and concurrency APIs when their contracts meet domain needs.
Consult current Java 21 API documentation for behavior and version availability before choosing a utility.
Avoid custom code merely because the existing API name is unfamiliar; write adapters to express domain-specific constraints.
Evaluate high-quality third-party libraries when the JDK does not fit, including compatibility, licensing and security maintenance.
nuance: Java 21 introduces java.util.random.RandomGenerator families and bounded overloads; select algorithm based on context rather than claiming one legacy generator universally fastest.
ThreadLocalRandom is appropriate for ordinary concurrent non-cryptographic random values, but never for authentication secrets.
SplittableRandom is designed for splittable pseudorandom streams; parallel execution does not guarantee stable ordering or reproducibility.
InputStream.transferTo moves bytes but does not close input/output streams; resource ownership and close failures remain caller responsibilities.
Even a standard API can violate a domain assumption (nulls, modification, thread safety, output ownership); verify its documented contract.
A cryptographic provider has additional entropy and lifecycle considerations; reproducibility tests should use deterministic PRNGs, not assert SecureRandom output.
notes.misconception: If a utility is already part of java.util, it must be both cryptographically secure and optimal for every workload.
notes.production_context: A voucher generator uses SecureRandom for unguessable redemption tokens, while a load-test simulator uses a seeded non-security PRNG and a bounded API for deterministic replay.
notes.java21_delta: Java 21 offers RandomGenerator factory APIs and additional standard utilities beyond the Java 9-era book; never repeat publication-era speed ratios or blanket Random-versus-ThreadLocalRandom guidance as universal modern facts.
